title: The Map That Changed the World: William Smith and the Birth of Modern Geology
author: Simon Winchester
target_audience: General readers interested in science and history
Readers curious about the development of scientific thought
Educators looking for accessible science history
core_themes: The life and struggles of William Smith
The birth and evolution of modern geology
The significance of maps and data in science
Social mobility and class barriers in 18th-19th century England
The intersection of science, society, and recognition
primary_purpose: To narrate the dramatic and inspiring story of William Smith, who overcame social and financial obstacles to create the world's first geological map, and in doing so, laid the foundation for the science of geology and transformed the way humans understand the earth.

structure_format.narrative_style: Engaging, descriptive, and narrative-driven, blending biography with scientific explanation
structure_format.organization: Chronological, interweaving Smith's life events, scientific discoveries, and their historical context
features: Detailed historical context of 18th- and 19th-century England
Explications of geological science for general audiences

key_concepts_lessons: Individual perseverance can shape the course of scientific history.
Scientific innovation often comes from outside traditional academic circles.
Mapping and visual data are powerful tools in scientific discovery.
Social class and institutional power significantly impact the recognition of new knowledge.
Science can transform not only ideas, but also economies and societies.
Recognition may be slow, but foundational work ultimately prevails.
notable_features: Biographical focus on a lesser-known but pivotal figure in science
Blends scientific explanation with historical narrative
Illustrates the cultural and social context of scientific discovery
Contains reproductions of Smith's geological map
Explores the legacy of a foundational scientific tool
cultural_historical_context: Set during the late 18th and early 19th centuries—an era of industrial change, class stratification, and scientific revolution in England, the book traces Smith’s struggles as a working-class outsider seeking acceptance and recognition in an elite scientific community. Published in 2001 at a time of broad pop-science interest, it highlights how foundational discoveries often arise from overlooked individuals.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for bringing scientific history to a mainstream audience
Celebrated for its narrative style and ability to humanize science
Used in classrooms and referenced in popular science writing
Helped revive interest in William Smith and the history of geological mapping
Praised for its accessibility to non-specialists; some geologists have critiqued minor technical inaccuracies
